bibliographic.title: AI and the Transformation of Accountability and Discretion in Urban Governance
bibliographic.citation_apa: Goldsmith, S., & Yang, J. (2026). AI and the Transformation of Accountability and Discretion in Urban Governance. Urban Governance. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ugj.2026.02.005

methodology.method_family: conceptual analysis with illustrative cases drawing on public administration theory and algorithmic governance research
methodology.technology_context: AI broadly in urban governance, including chatbots, virtual assistants, conversational AI, GenAI, LLMs, IoT, digital twins, and municipal service-delivery systems

eligibility.decision_rationale: The article is primarily a conceptual analysis of how AI reshapes discretion and accountability in urban governance, not an empirical or technical study of conversational LLM governance. It is relevant as foundational/contextual evidence because it explicitly discusses GenAI, LLMs, chatbots, virtual assistants, risks such as bias and opacity, and proposes principles including human-led decision-making and citizen-engaged oversight in public-sector settings.
eligibility.manual_spotcheck_reason: Only front matter, abstract, introduction fragments, and keyword-hit excerpts were provided; full methods, limitations, and governance-principles sections were not visible for complete appraisal.

appraisal.notes: Appropriate for a conceptual governance paper, but primary empirical sampling, data-collection procedures, and ethics/reflexivity are not described in the supplied text. Claims rely on theory plus illustrative secondary cases rather than original empirical investigation.

cerqual.explanation: The argument is coherent and clearly framed around accountability, discretion, and urban governance, with explicit links to GenAI, LLMs, and conversational tools. Confidence is moderate rather than high because the supplied text shows a conceptual design with illustrative cases and incomplete visibility into methods, limitations, and detailed operational governance mechanisms for conversational LLM systems.

synthesis.main_claim: AI, including GenAI and LLM-based tools, does not simply restrict or enhance bureaucratic discretion but redistributes it across institutional levels, professional roles, and citizen interactions, thereby transforming multiple forms of accountability in urban governance.
synthesis.contribution: Introduces the concept of accountable discretion and proposes guiding principles linked to actionable measures, including equal AI access, adaptive administrative structures, robust data governance, proactive human-led decision-making, and citizen-engaged oversight.
synthesis.use_in_review: Use as foundational/contextual evidence for governance of AI in regulated public-sector environments. Useful for framing how conversational tools such as chatbots and virtual assistants relate to accountability, oversight, and discretion, but not as central empirical evidence on conversational LLM governance mechanisms such as guardrails, observability, or post-deployment monitoring.
